attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his own newsletter, in his own voice.

semantics.note: Firm retrospective claim with no hedge. The normalisation keeps 'almost every', 'major thinker', 'come around' and the 2019 baseline.

contract.note: Marcus named no measure. Reading the critique as 'scaling language prediction alone is insufficient' is the ordinary reading his context supports, and it is not stretched either way. It is fair, but who counts as a major thinker and what 'almost every' means are undefined, so the result turns on interpretation.

evidence.note: Bengio (2023) doubts that scaling fixes reliability. This shows overlap for one leading researcher, but not near-universality or a change of mind.
Hassabis (July 2025) puts it at 50/50 whether scaling suffices and says there is lots of room to scale. That weakens one of Marcus's named examples but is not a census.
Hinton (June 2025) argues LLMs understand language. This is a different question from whether scaling is sufficient, so it is only indirect.
A broad expert synthesis (Jan 2025) records disagreement over whether scaling resolves remaining limits. It points against consensus but predates the end of the period and does not count adherents.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no representative population or survey of leading researchers and no before-and-after chronology. One researcher (Bengio) overlaps with the critique. Hassabis's 50/50 view and the expert disagreement recorded in e4 cast doubt on near-universality, but they do not show that a substantial body clearly rejects the critique. The evidence meets neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition.
